title: Genesis of High‐Fluoride Groundwater and Associated Health Risks in the Huangqihai Basin
content:
In the Huangqihai Basin, mineral dissolution (48.7%) and competitive adsorption (42.2%) are the primary drivers of groundwater fluoride enrichment, with infants facing the highest health risks—underscoring the urgent need for targeted water management in semiarid regions.


ABSTRACT

The presence of high fluoride in groundwater poses a major health concern. In the present study, 63 samples of groundwater and surface water were obtained from the Huangqihai Basin in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The influencing factors and their relative contributions to fluoride (F−) enrichment in groundwater were analyzed, and the potential health risks associated with groundwater fluoride were assessed. Studies of groundwater samples from the Huangqihai Basin indicate that high-fluoride groundwater is mainly concentrated in the middle and lower reaches of the basin. This study employed an integrated approach combining hydrogeochemical analysis and machine learning to identify the main driving factors and their contribution rates to fluoride enrichment in the basin. The enrichment of F− in groundwater within the study area is primarily controlled by mineral dissolution–precipitation, while competitive adsorption, cation exchange, and evaporation are secondary contributors. Hydrogeochemical analysis indicates that the hydrogeochemical types of the samples are predominantly HCO₃-Ca, Ca-Mg-Cl mixed type, and Ca-Na-HCO₃ mixed type. In this study, a Random Forest model (RF) was employed, with SI fluorite, HCO₃−, pH, Q ce, and Cl/(Cl+HCO₃) selected as predictor variables, to fit and predict fluoride (F−) concentrations in groundwater. Based on the feature importance scores output by the model, the relative contribution rates of each driving factor to F− enrichment were quantified. Quantitative attribution showed that mineral dissolution–precipitation, competitive adsorption, cation exchange, and evaporation accounted for 48.72%, 42.16%, 7.43%, and 1.69% of groundwater F− enrichment, respectively. In addition, the health risk assessment identified the middle and lower reaches of the basin as high-risk areas, with infants and children being the most sensitive groups. These results provide a scientific foundation for the effective management of high-F− groundwater and for safeguarding drinking water supplies for local communities, highlighting the need for targeted water supply management and long-term monitoring.
